title: §11-003: Proxy, Composite & Decorator Patterns
description: Multiple-choice practice questions and deep runtime verification for §11-003 (Proxy, Composite & Decorator Patterns).

cards.concept: Proxy, Composite & Decorator Patterns: Proxy & Reflect Structural Pattern
cards.question: How do `Proxy` and `Reflect` enable non-invasive structural interception (such as metrics logging or validation) in Node.js services?

options.text: They compile JavaScript objects into C++ binary shared libraries.
Proxy intercepts fundamental object operations via handler traps, while Reflect forwards the default operation with proper receiver binding.
They run on a separate V8 thread isolate automatically.
They serialize objects to disk before each method invocation.

cards.explanation: The Proxy object allows wrapping targets to intercept property lookups, method calls, and assignments. Reflect provides static methods that perform default behaviors, preserving `this` context via receiver.
cards.pitfall: Failing to pass `receiver` to Reflect.get breaks getter methods that rely on the proxy's `this` context.
cards.citation: MDN Web Docs: Proxy & Reflect / JavaScript Design Patterns

cards.concept: Proxy, Composite & Decorator Patterns: Module Caching & The Singleton Pattern
cards.question: How does Node.js enforce the Singleton pattern natively across CommonJS and ESM module imports?

options.text: By locking the file with OS file mutexes during read.
By caching the resolved module exports in `require.cache` after initial evaluation, returning the identical cached instance on subsequent imports.
By storing singletons in Redis by default.
By refusing to load a module more than once per user session.

cards.explanation: Node.js caches modules by resolved absolute filename. The first require/import evaluates the module; subsequent calls return the cached export, naturally creating a singleton.
cards.pitfall: If two packages resolve different case-sensitive paths or different versions in node_modules, module caching creates multiple instances, breaking the singleton.
